items.title: Opus 5.5 AI agents identify two candidate room-temperature magnetic semiconductors with potential spintronic applications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Opus 5.5 agents discover two room-temperature magnetic semiconductor candidates
items.summary:
A team using Opus 5.5 AI agents has discovered two candidate materials for room-temperature magnetic semiconductors, which could advance spintronic technology by enabling efficient electron spin sorting without macroscopic magnetic fields. One candidate was newly designed by the AI agents, while the other was first synthesized in 1999 and predicted by calculations to have the desired properties.

The research focuses on materials that combine features of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, specifically Luttinger compensated magnets, which allow spin-up and spin-down electrons to be sorted by energy despite having zero net magnetic moment. This property could improve data storage speed and density by overcoming limitations of traditional magnetic materials used in spintronics.

items.title: Reflection introduces Beam, a 501 billion parameter open-weight sparse Mixture-of-Experts model optimized for coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks with high compute reinforcement learning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beam: Reflection's 501B open-weight model
items.summary:
Reflection has launched Beam, its first open-weight model featuring 501 billion total parameters with 23 billion active, designed for coding, reasoning, and agentic workloads. Beam was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens from diverse, high-quality datasets and underwent extensive reinforcement learning using 10.5K NVIDIA GPUs over four weeks, achieving competitive performance with greater inference efficiency compared to similar-sized open models.

Beam emphasizes efficiency and capability, delivering strong coding and reasoning performance while using 3 to 4 times less inference compute than comparable models. The model incorporates a controllable reasoning effort parameter allowing users to balance response length and performance. Reflection plans to release Beam's weights, technical report, and developer tools later this month after final evaluations and red-teaming.

items.originalTitle: AI Whistleblowers Say Researchers Are Checking AI Less Frequently
items.summary:
Three former AI researchers testified at a New York City Council hearing that AI labs have increasingly allowed AI to drive coding and research processes, resulting in less frequent human checks of AI-generated work. The whistleblowers, formerly of Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind, highlighted changes in AI research practices that may affect oversight and quality control.

Anthropic reported that as of August, AI was leading over 25% of its model research and development, reflecting a broader trend of AI accelerating research workflows. Representatives from the AI labs did not directly address the whistleblowers' claims during the hearing.

items.originalSummary:
It won’t be any surprise to people with human intelligence that Monday’s New York City Council hearing on the risks of AI was as theatrical as a Broadway show. What was more surprising was what the AI researchers testified about how AI research is evolving, and what that means for their job.

For those who missed it, the city council heard testimony from three AI lab whistleblowers: Jacob Coxon, formerly of Anthropic and OpenAI; Alex Turner, formerly of Google DeepMind; and Daniel Kokotajlo, formerly of OpenAI. Afterwards, they heard from representatives of the AI labs. We’ll get to that lower down.

One of the most interesting parts of the whistleblowers’ testimony related to the AI research process. Coxon and Kokotajlo each said that researchers at the labs have lately been letting AI drive the process of writing code and research. Researchers check AI’s work less frequently, they said.

The labs might not agree with that exact characterization, although their representatives weren’t asked about it at the hearing. But the labs have been the first to say that AI has greatly accelerated the process of AI research. Anthropic even said in a report last month that, as of August, AI was leading more than a quarter of model research and development at the company.

items.title: LibreOffice commits to no AI integration in default software to protect user privacy and data control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LibreOffice says ‘no AI’ is now a software feature
items.summary:
The Document Foundation, which develops the open source LibreOffice document editor, announced it will not include AI features in its default software configuration to ensure user privacy and data security. The organization emphasized that LibreOffice does not upload documents to external servers and functions without requiring a network connection, allowing users to retain full control over their data.

LibreOffice allows users to add AI capabilities through optional extensions that connect to local AI models, but the foundation currently sees no AI integration meeting its criteria for privacy and independence from single AI providers. This stance contrasts with many software makers who are rapidly incorporating AI features, often involving data processing on remote servers.

items.originalTitle: Why the SaaSpocalypse Isn’t Over For Workday
items.summary: Workday’s enterprise applications remain essential for storing employee and financial data, but AI technologies are limiting their growth potential. Some customers use AI agents from providers like Anthropic and Microsoft to extract and analyze Workday data directly, reducing the need to interact with Workday’s own interface. Additionally, many companies with access to Workday’s AI-enhanced tools reportedly do not use them regularly, according to consultants working with thousands of Workday clients.

items.originalSummary:
AI doesn’t seem likely to completely replace enterprise apps like Workday, which companies use to store key information about employees and financial transactions. But it is putting potential constraints on their growth.

Already, some Workday customers are using so-called AI agents from Anthropic, Microsoft and other providers to pull data from Workday so they can analyze employment records or trends, for example, meaning the customers themselves don’t have to visit the app. And many companies that pay for access to Workday’s own AI tools, which sit on top of its core HR and finance databases, aren’t regularly using them, according to interviews with five consultants and partners that work with more than 2,000 Workday customers.

items.originalTitle: EmbeddingGemma 2: an open, lightweight multimodal embedding model
items.summary:
Google DeepMind introduced EmbeddingGemma 2, an open-source multimodal embedding model that unifies text, images, audio, and video into a shared embedding space for on-device use. The model, built on the Gemma 4 architecture with 740 million parameters, supports efficient local processing with a focus on privacy, enabling applications like semantic search and retrieval across multiple data types without cloud dependency.

EmbeddingGemma 2 offers modular design with optional encoders for vision and audio, supports dynamic vector dimension reduction for storage efficiency, and features an extended 8K token context window for processing longer inputs. It achieves top-tier performance on benchmarks for code, vision, and audio tasks among sub-1B parameter models, and is optimized to run within tight resource constraints on devices such as the Google Pixel 11 Pro.

The model facilitates on-device retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipelines when paired with generative models like Gemma 4, enabling complex multimodal understanding and real-time decision-making. Developers can access the model weights on platforms like Hugging Face and Kaggle, with tools and APIs provided to support deployment and integration in privacy-sensitive applications.

items.originalTitle: AI Is Now Si: Super Intelligence Isn't Superior
items.summary:
A US executive order signed on September 29, 2026, requires federal agencies to use the term "Super Intelligence" (SI) instead of "Artificial Intelligence" (AI) in all official communications, arguing that current AI systems exceed mere imitation of human intelligence. Despite the renaming, the legal definition remains unchanged, describing SI as machine-based systems that make predictions or decisions based on human-defined objectives, identical to the previous AI definition.

The change reflects a broader trend in Silicon Valley, with companies like Meta and Microsoft adopting the term "superintelligence" for their AI initiatives. However, in AI research, superintelligence still refers to a hypothetical machine surpassing human capabilities across virtually all tasks, which has not yet been achieved. The article also discusses the symbolic implications of renaming AI to SI, comparing it to historical examples of misattributed creation and emphasizing that current AI systems are fundamentally human-made.

items.summary: A recent study evaluated the humor capabilities of six Frontier AI language models by having human raters assess original jokes generated using random word pairs. The experiment aimed to determine if advances in AI's verifiable skills like math and coding also translate to subjective domains such as joke creation. Results showed that larger, more recent models like GPT-6, Fable 5.1, and Opus 4.5 produced jokes rated as funnier compared to older or smaller models. The study used blind human ratings to compare jokes and enforced originality by requiring specific word inclusion, avoiding country-specific references. This suggests AI humor is improving over time, though challenges remain in ensuring truly original and universally funny content.

items.title: Mistral launches Large 4, a trillion-parameter AI model trained in Europe focused on cybersecurity tasks avoided by US models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mistral Large 4 is Europe's trillion-parameter answer to US models that refuse security work
items.summary:
Mistral has introduced Large 4, its largest AI model with one trillion parameters, trained on European infrastructure and designed to handle cybersecurity tasks that US models like Claude and GPT-6 avoid due to safety filters. The model is currently available in preview via Mistral Studio, with full weights expected by the end of October. An independent Intelligence Index scores Large 4 at 38 points, a significant improvement over previous Mistral models but still behind leading closed models such as Claude Opus 5.5.

Large 4 excels in reproducing and patching software vulnerabilities, scoring 82 percent on a cybersecurity benchmark where competitors score near zero because they refuse such tasks. Mistral emphasizes that this capability addresses a gap in security research, as closed models block vulnerability work despite attackers exploiting them. The model also performs well in coding and image understanding benchmarks and is designed to run in private clouds or on-premises, supporting European data sovereignty.

Mistral is currently collaborating with security firms, partners, and government agencies to test and refine Large 4, aiming to balance security capabilities with high refusal rates on malicious prompts. The company positions Large 4 as a European alternative to US and Chinese AI models, particularly for sensitive cybersecurity applications where access to open-weight models is critical.

items.originalTitle: Quoting Felix Rieseberg
items.summary:
The "old" version of Cowork runs model inference in the cloud, executing tool calls in an Anthropic-provided VM we shipped to your computer. We added the VM for capability, safety, and security reasons - mapping in just the data you explicitly added to your session. People loved what they were able to do with Claude but didn't love the disk, battery, and performance cost of running the VM locally. Also, people didn't love that closing your laptop means the work stops.

The "new" version of Cowork runs model inference and the VM in the cloud. Each session gets its own sandbox, not sharing state with other sessions. When the VM needs something on the users' device (like a file), the desktop app is responsible for that file access tool call. [...]

We think this solves a lot of problems we've heard about (like using Cowork from a phone, keeping work running, or getting all the same power without losing battery to the VM)

— Felix Rieseberg, Anthropic, see also this help page
